summary: At 3,314 square miles, Monterey County is larger than Rhode Island and Delaware combined, yet only 132 people occupy each square mile — a figure that makes sense the moment you realize the county stretches from the dramatic Big Sur coastline through the Salinas Valley, one of the most productive agricultural corridors on Earth, sometimes called "the Salad Bowl of the World" for its staggering output of lettuce, strawberries, and broccoli. That agricultural engine, alongside a military presence anchored by the Defense Language Institute and former Fort Ord, and a tourism economy fed by Cannery Row, the Monterey Bay Aquarium, and Pebble Beach, means employment is unusually spread across sectors — but switching industries without a long commute can be tricky when jobs cluster in distinct pockets separated by twenty miles of farmland. The median home value of $723,100 against a median household income of $94,486 yields a price-to-income ratio above 7.6, which pushes ownership out of comfortable reach at the median; median rent at $1,995 is more manageable but still claims roughly a quarter of gross monthly income. Daily highs average a remarkably mild 71°F year-round with nearly 9.6 hours of sunshine, and the coastal fog that rolls through the western towns burns off to reveal a landscape that swings from Pacific bluffs to oak-studded foothills within a single afternoon's drive. The essential tension is that Monterey County offers world-class scenery and mild weather stapled to an economy where the dominant industries — agriculture, defense, hospitality — don't always generate the incomes the housing market demands.
